tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The README quote is verbatim but has no methodology. However, the well-known independent lzbench suite (public code, inikep/lzbench, 1.1k stars) benchmarks zlib-ng 2.2.3 against zlib 1.3.1 on Silesia, using gcc 14.2.0 on an AMD EPYC 9554, and zlib-ng wins at every level. It is not A because the page gives the compiler but not the build flags (they are only implicit in the Makefile defaults).

corrections.claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.0.1 (AMD EPYC 9554, gcc 14.2.0, Silesia, single thread), zlib-ng 2.2.3 vs zlib 1.3.1. Compression: 202 vs 93.0 MB/s at -1, 62.1 vs 25.3 MB/s at -6, 24.6 vs 10.3 MB/s at -9 (~2.2-2.5x). Decompression: 471-518 vs 323-348 MB/s (~1.5x) (ratios derived from page data). The project README separately claims "x86-64 can be about 4x faster than stock zlib".
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 14.2.0 (lzbench 2.0.1 build). Flags are not stated on the page; the lzbench Makefile defaults to -O3 -DNDEBUG.
corrections.hardware: AMD EPYC 9554 @ 3.10 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 24.04.1
corrections.is_fork_of: https://github.com/madler/zlib (hard fork per README 'motivation for this fork'; not a GitHub fork)
corrections.caveats: The README's "about 4x" claim gives no CPU, compiler or flags, and lzbench does not reproduce it. lzbench shows about 2.2-2.5x faster compression and about 1.5x faster decompression than zlib 1.3.1, and at level -1 zlib-ng gets a clearly worse ratio (44.41% vs 36.45%). lzbench does not measure CRC32/Adler32 on their own, so the checksum SIMD gains rest only on first-party code (the Google Benchmark suite in the repo) with no published numbers. The lzbench results table used zlib-ng 2.2.3, while the current lzbench bundles 2.3.3.

notes: Metadata checked via gh: license Zlib, not archived, GitHub fork=false, 2100 stars, last commit 2026-09-25, so it is active. The README quote is accurate, but the tier is raised to B on the strength of the independent lzbench table. The claimed speedup is rewritten to lzbench's numbers, and the README's 4x is kept only as a quoted first-party claim.
